How to use this map−
What this shows. Legislative accountability means the ways the public can watch and check the people who make the law — how legislators vote and are lobbied, campaign finance and asset disclosures, freedom-of-information regimes, and the watchdogs and records that keep law-making transparent — plus the statutes themselves. This map plots those sources for every country — and for every state, county or municipality where data exists — alongside legislatures and civic buildings worldwide.

How complete is it? Two honest measures — raw (share of all units on Earth at that tier, most of which publish nothing) and realistic (share of units that plausibly have a discoverable official source). These figures are within this map's scope — legislative accountability (law-making and the bodies that watch it); they do not measure executive, judicial or other branches of government. Every URL is verified; nothing is invented.
LevelOn map% of raw% realistic
International90 bodies~78%~95%
National200 / 200~100%~92%
State / province3,880+~100%~97%
County / district17,000+~37%~74%
Municipal100,000+~40%~85%
The low raw figures for counties and municipalities reflect real-world absence — most of the world's ~47,000 counties and ~250,000 municipalities publish nothing online. A blank lower-tier unit means “no source found,” not “unchecked.” Realistic figures below the national line are estimates (±15 pts) and sit near the ceiling of what is machine-verifiable.

Navigate. Click a country to zoom in — its first-level regions load and any that hold sources light up. Click a lit region to open a list of its legislators, vote records, watchdogs and other sources, and to drill deeper into its sub-divisions (state → county → municipal). Click empty space or zoom out to step back up.

The coloured dots are physical buildings, not the sources above — town halls, parliaments and accountability offices, plotted so you can see where law-making actually happens. Zoom in to see them: ● blue = town halls, ● yellow = parliaments, ● green = audit, ● purple = electoral, ● orange = ombudsman — zoom in, then click a dot for its name & link (toggle them off, top-right, to browse regions freely).

Two ways to filter:
1· Lens pills (right) — each lens is a kind of accountability (legislators, votes & bills, lobbying, campaign finance, asset disclosure, the laws themselves…). Selecting one filters the map to that theme: only countries and regions that actually hold a source of that type stay highlighted, the rest dim, so you can see coverage and gaps at a glance. Below the pills you can narrow further by source type, trust, media and voice.
2· This index (below) — the full directory of every source on the map. Group & sort it with the two drop-downs (by country, level, lens, source type…) and search by name in the filter box.

🌐 Global Wire
The legislative climate — a standing overview, with a live wire beneath drawn from a rotating selection of 150+ of the world’s leading accountability news sources (not all of them).
Before ~1700. For most of history, law was whatever rulers decreed, and it mostly encoded hierarchy: conquest, bondage, the exclusion of the many. Yet in many societies bodies arose to advise or restrain the ruler — councils, assemblies, gatherings of elders — each planting the same seed: that some rule stood above the ruler and could bind even them.

1700s–1800s. An idea then hardened into doctrine: that law should rest on universal rights and the consent of the governed. Yet the same powers that proclaimed liberty also legislated slavery, empire and the exclusion of women and the poor — rights declared and denied in the same breath.

1800s–1945. Legislatures began undoing their worst injustices — abolishing slavery, slowly widening the vote — before the deepest fall: parliaments and decrees turned law itself into an instrument of oppression, from racial and colonial statutes to the Nuremberg Laws and the machinery of dictatorship. Atrocity was made lawful.

1945–2000s. The recoil was historic: as the number of sovereign states multiplied, the elected legislature became, for the first time, a genuinely worldwide institution. The era built a human-rights order, civil-rights and anti-discrimination laws and entrenched protections — then added environmental, consumer and privacy law, and the first tools made to keep lawmakers honest: freedom-of-information acts, audit offices and public registers.

Today (2010s–now). The needle no longer points one way. Independent trackers (V-Dem, Freedom House) record over 15 years of net democratic decline, and it tends to follow three patterns rather than a single dramatic coup. First, capture by the elected: a leader wins power fairly, then uses the legislature’s own majority to rewrite the rules in their favour. Second, the legislature sidelined: parliaments are dissolved, bypassed or reduced to rubber stamps while real power moves to the president. Third, quiet erosion inside healthy democracies: no single blow, but the slow weakening of the tools that keep lawmakers honest — gerrymandered districts, starved freedom-of-information laws, captured watchdogs and gridlock, the pattern most visible across parts of the United States and Europe. Running the other way is a steady counter-current of reform: the European Union tightening lobbying rules and passing the first broad AI law, and dozens of countries adopting registers of who owns companies and what officials are worth. The meter reads strain, not collapse — the machinery of accountability stands strong on paper while the will to honour it wears thin.

Veins to watch. The hollowing of a legislature rarely announces itself; it arrives as procedural “reforms” that each sound reasonable alone. Watch who gets in: districts redrawn to lock in a majority or left grossly unequal in size (gerrymandering, as in contested US state maps; malapportionment, as in over-weighted rural seats), electoral thresholds raised to shut out smaller parties (Turkey long imposed a 10% bar), registration rules, ID requirements and voter-roll purges that quietly thin the electorate, opposition candidates disqualified or whole parties banned and dissolved (Cambodia dissolved its main opposition in 2017), and voting systems rewritten between elections by the very people they will favour (Hungary’s 2011 overhaul) — until the make-up of the chamber is settled before a single ballot is cast. Watch how law is made: bills rushed through without hearings, committee scrutiny skipped, omnibus and “emergency” measures voted at midnight (thousand-page US omnibus bills), debate guillotined, and whole programmes enacted by decree, ordinance or emergency order that bypass the floor entirely (India’s ordinance route; pandemic emergency powers) — the legislature present in form but absent in fact. Watch what is hidden in the making: unrecorded, proxy or bloc votes that erase individual responsibility, closed sessions, riders and earmarks slipped in unread, laws passed and then left unpublished or backdated, and freedom-of-information regimes hollowed by sweeping exemptions, prohibitive fees and endless delay (India’s 2019 RTI dilution) so no one can reconstruct who decided what, and for whom. Watch who shapes the vote: undisclosed and dark money in campaigns (US super-PAC spending), lobbying conducted off any register, the revolving door between legislator, staffer and lobbyist (Brussels and Washington alike), foreign influence routed through cut-outs and front groups (“foreign agent” scandals), gifts, junkets and sinecures, and conflicts of interest and outside earnings left undeclared — until a lawmaker’s incentives quietly belong to someone other than the voter. Watch whether anyone can check them: audit offices, ombudsmen, information commissioners and anti-corruption agencies starved of budget, packed with loyalists or simply ignored (Guatemala’s CICIG shut down in 2019), ethics committees that never sit, subpoenas defied and inquiries stonewalled, asset-declaration rules watered down or unenforced, and parliamentary immunity stretched from a shield for free debate into blanket impunity for those in power (self-amnesties). Watch the independence of the chamber itself: parliaments dissolved, suspended or reduced to rubber-stamping an executive (Tunisia’s 2021 shutdown; Russia’s managed Duma), sittings cancelled and elections postponed, term limits removed by the very body they bind (scrapped across several states to extend rule), immunity stripped selectively to prosecute and jail opposition members, party discipline and defection laws used to crush independent votes, staff, research and budgets cut until the legislature can no longer draft or scrutinise on its own, and constitutions amended — often in a single rushed session — to entrench a majority beyond the reach of the next election (Venezuela’s 2017 Constituent Assembly). Any one of these can carry an innocent explanation. Where several appear together, and especially where they all move the same way within a single term of office, the legislature’s independence is usually being hollowed from the inside.

Subcategories
▾On the map
Parliament / legislature
National & state law-making chambers — parliaments, congresses, assemblies, senates. The lawmakers themselves; the seat of the legislative branch you hold to account.
Town hall / council
City & municipal councils — local legislators who pass ordinances and budgets; the legislature closest to residents.
Audit institution
Auditors-general & courts of accounts — independent bodies that check how the money a legislature votes is actually spent.
Electoral body
Election commissions & electoral tribunals — run and referee the votes that seat legislators in the first place.
Ombudsman
Public-complaints offices — investigate maladministration and defend citizens against government and legislative overreach.
County / regional council
County, regional & district councils — the legislative tier between national and city (boards of supervisors, county commissions).
International body
Cross-border legislative & transparency organisations — inter-parliamentary unions, regional assemblies and global monitoring networks that watch law-making across nations. Click any gold marker to open it, just like a country.
